sections.heading: Why we are writing to you

sentences.text: We are writing because PCDH19-related epileptic encephalopathy early infantile and SLC6A1-related epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures are both recorded on the same mechanism road: too little protein from loss of function of one copy.
The reported phenotype similarity is high, but the shared features are broad seizure terms, so we want to be careful and specific.
Both gene-disease links are listed as definitive in Gene2Phenotype.
Both conditions are recorded with inferred loss of function as the disease mechanism.
The shared informative features listed are atonic seizure, generalized non-motor (absence) seizure, generalized-onset motor seizure, non-motor seizure, and myoclonic seizure.
Registry design and natural history protocol are marked as transferable from the SLC6A1 community to ours.
Outcome measures and endpoints are also marked as transferable, with review of age of onset and severity before any tool is adopted.
Clinical network, sites, and investigators are marked as transferable as a starting point.

sections.heading: What we would like to learn from or reuse

sentences.text: We would like to learn from the SLC6A1-NDD Prospective Longitudinal Natural History Study and from Simons Searchlight as examples of registry or natural history structure.
We would like to understand which data items, visit schedule, and measured domains have been most useful in practice.
We would also like to learn which sites and investigators have experience across these seizure and neurodevelopmental conditions.
For research planning, disease models and assays may offer reusable ideas, but only with expert review.
For future study planning, trial design may be a useful template, but it also needs expert review.
For PCDH19, no registry or natural history study was found in the sources searched.
For SLC6A1, two such studies were found: NCT07531511 and NCT01238250.
For PCDH19, no targeted clinical trial was found in the sources searched.
For SLC6A1, three targeted trials were found: NCT07173153, NCT04937062, and NCT07847918.
No approved disease-specific therapy was found for either condition.
We must not assume that a therapy approach, a model, or a trial design transfers directly just because the two conditions are on the same road.
The reason is that mechanism is recorded per gene and disease, not per family, and a child's own variant may act differently.
Our families should confirm the variant class with a clinical geneticist before acting on transfer ideas.
We also must not assume eligibility for an SLC6A1 trial, because enrolment in the neighbor's trial is not asserted.
The listed SLC6A1 organization is unverified, and its registry status is unknown.
The shared phenotype signal also has an important limit: 100% of the shared weight comes from common, low-information terms.
The curated mechanism for both conditions is inferred from variant types rather than direct functional evidence.
Does the overlap between PCDH19 and SLC6A1 go beyond common features such as seizures and developmental delay, in your clinical experience.
Is SLC6A1 Connect the right contact, and does it run a registry.
Has a child's specific PCDH19 variant been functionally classified as loss of function, gain of function, or dominant negative, and does it match the mechanism recorded for the condition.
What functional evidence exists for PCDH19, given that the curated mechanism is inferred from variant types.
Thank you for reading.

glossary.meaning: A gene change that reduces how well the gene works.
A study that follows people over time to learn how a condition changes.
A way to track symptoms, skills, or daily function in a study.
A doctor with specialist training in genetic conditions and variant interpretation.
A cell or animal system used to study a condition in research.
